items.title: How central Gaza became a chain of refugee camps, and a front line again
items.thread: Gaza ceasefire and Board of Peace plan
items.hook: Israel's first large operation in central Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire is unfolding near the yellow line, in a district of refugee camps founded in 1949. The [[p:Board of Peace]] warns the truce could collapse; the area's history explains why this ground is so crowded and so contested.
items.body:
Central Gaza is a short stretch of a narrow strip: the town of Deir al-Balah and three refugee camps, Nuseirat, Bureij and Maghazi, packed between the Wadi Gaza and Khan Younis. Israel's new operation there, near the "yellow line", lands on ground whose shape was set by wars, refugees and roads.

Before 1948 this was farmland around a small market town. During the [[e:1948 Arab–Israeli War]], about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were driven from their homes, a loss Palestinians call the [[e:Nakba]]. Many from villages east and north of Gaza, such as Falouja, ended up in the coastal pocket held by Egypt's army. Aid workers in early 1949 found them in tents, old British barracks and fields; within a year Maghazi and its neighbours were organized camps. The UN created [[p:UNRWA]] {{note: Set up by UN General Assembly Resolution 302 in December 1949; it began operating in May 1950.}} to feed, school and shelter them, and refugees soon outnumbered Gaza's original residents.

The [[e:1949 Armistice Agreements]] froze the front line. Egypt ran the strip under military administration without granting its people citizenship, apart from a brief Israeli occupation during the [[e:Suez Crisis]]. Refugees lived within a day's walk of villages they could not return to. The camps became the heart of Palestinian political life, where the demand for a right of return was most personal and where armed groups later recruited.

Israel captured Gaza in the [[e:Six-Day War]] of 1967; a census that year found nearly half the population living in camps. In 1972 Israel founded the settlement of **Netzarim** just north of the central camps. It was small but strategic: protecting it meant controlling the roads across the strip, with checkpoints that could cut Gaza in two.

That arrangement ended with [[e:Israeli disengagement from Gaza|Israel's withdrawal]] in 2005, when about 9,000 settlers and the army left. [[p:Hamas]] won Palestinian elections in 2006 and seized the strip from Fatah in 2007; Israel and Egypt then tightened a blockade.

The old geography returned in the [[e:Gaza war]]. Days after invading in October 2023, Israeli troops cut a road across the strip through the former Netzarim site, the **Netzarim Corridor**, splitting north from south. The central camps sat just below it, and Israel repeatedly told northerners to move south, swelling Deir al-Balah with displaced families. Israel left the corridor during the January 2025 truce and returned when it broke down in March.

The [[e:Gaza peace plan|October 2025 ceasefire]] {{note: Took effect on 10 October 2025 under Donald Trump's 20-point plan, after talks mediated by Egypt, Qatar and Turkey.}} pulled Israeli forces back to the yellow line, leaving them in about 53% of Gaza while most of its roughly two million people crowded west of it, including in the central camps. Hamas has not disarmed, Israel has not withdrawn further, and the [[p:Board of Peace]] now warns the truce could collapse. A push near the line in central Gaza tests whether it is a temporary stage or a new border.

timeline.text: About 700,000 Palestinians are displaced in the [[e:1948 Arab–Israeli War]]; many crowd into the Egyptian-held coastal strip.
The [[e:1949 Armistice Agreements]] freeze the lines; camps such as Maghazi take shape, and the UN creates [[p:UNRWA]] in December.
Israel captures Gaza in the [[e:Six-Day War]]; nearly half its people live in camps.
Israel founds the Netzarim settlement just north of the central camps.
[[e:Israeli disengagement from Gaza|Israel withdraws]] its settlers and troops; [[p:Hamas]] takes over the strip two years later.
In the [[e:Gaza war]], Israeli forces cut the Netzarim Corridor across the strip, just north of the central camps.
The [[e:Gaza peace plan|ceasefire]] takes effect; Israel pulls back to the yellow line, holding about 53% of Gaza.
Israel launches a concentrated operation in three areas of central Gaza near the yellow line; the [[p:Board of Peace]] warns the truce could collapse.

perspectives.view: The central camps are living proof of the [[e:Nakba]]: families expelled in 1948 and never allowed home, then occupied, blockaded and bombed. Israel's lines across Gaza, from Netzarim to the yellow line, are seen as tools to divide and shrink the territory, and the new operation as a breach of the ceasefire.

Israel says the 1948 refugee problem grew out of a war Arab states and forces launched, and that Gaza after 2005 was handed a chance it used to build [[p:Hamas]]'s military machine. Holding ground near the yellow line and striking fighters is framed as necessary until Hamas disarms, as the ceasefire plan requires.

perspectives.side: Mediators and the Board of Peace
perspectives.view: The US-backed [[p:Board of Peace]] and the Egyptian, Qatari and Turkish mediators treat the yellow line as a temporary first-phase line, and fault both sides for stalling the moves to disarmament, a stabilization force and further Israeli withdrawal.

keyTerms.meaning: The line Israeli forces withdrew to under the first phase of the October 2025 ceasefire; Israel controls the roughly 53% of Gaza east of it.
An east–west military road Israel cut across Gaza in late 2023, named after a settlement evacuated in 2005; it split the north from the centre and south.
The UN agency created in 1949 to serve Palestinian refugees; it runs schools, clinics and services in Gaza's camps.
Gaza's main north–south highway, running inland through the central district; Israel closed parts of it for the new operation.

items.whyItMatters: Central Gaza's camps hold some of the most densely packed people in the strip, many already displaced several times, so any fighting there is costly. The operation tests whether the yellow line stays a temporary ceasefire line or hardens into a de facto border, as Netzarim's roads once did. Watch whether the [[p:Board of Peace]] can restart talks on Hamas disarmament and further Israeli withdrawal before the truce unravels.

items.title: Why Western Sahara's referendum never happened
items.hook: The [[p:Polisario Front]] has declared a general mobilisation, three weeks after the UN mission that watched the Morocco–Polisario ceasefire was shut down. That mission was set up in 1991 to hold a referendum on independence, and the story of why the vote never came explains why the desert is tense again.
items.body:
When Spain began to pull out of its desert colony in 1975, the people who lived there were promised a vote on their future. Fifty-one years later that vote has never happened, the UN mission created to hold it has just been wound up, and the [[p:Polisario Front]] has called its fighters to arms. To see why, start with how Spain left.

Spain had ruled the coast since 1884, and from the 1960s the UN pressed it to let the Sahrawi people decide whether to become independent. Morocco claimed the territory as part of a historic kingdom; Mauritania claimed the south. Young Sahrawis, impatient with both Madrid and their neighbours, founded the Polisario in May 1973 to fight for independence. In October 1975 the [[e:Advisory opinion on Western Sahara|International Court of Justice]] found old ties of allegiance between some tribes and Morocco's sultan, but no claim to sovereignty that could override self-determination. [[p:Hassan II of Morocco|King Hassan II]] read it as a win and, within weeks, sent some 350,000 unarmed Moroccans across the border in the [[e:Green March]] {{note: Began on 6 November 1975, organised by Hassan II; marchers carried flags and Qurans a few kilometres into the territory.}}.

With [[p:Francisco Franco]] on his deathbed, Spain gave way. The [[e:Madrid Accords]] of 14 November 1975 handed the territory's administration to Morocco and Mauritania, without the Sahrawis or a referendum. Tens of thousands of Sahrawis fled to camps near Tindouf in Algeria, where many of their descendants still live, and the Polisario proclaimed the [[p:Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic]] {{note: Proclaimed at Bir Lehlou on 27 February 1976, one day after Spain's formal departure.}} and went to war, backed by Algeria.

The [[e:Western Sahara War]] knocked Mauritania out by 1979, and Morocco took its share too. Morocco then changed the war's shape by building the [[p:Moroccan Western Sahara wall|berm]] {{note: A sand wall of roughly 2,700 km, built in stages between 1980 and 1987, lined with mines, radar and troops.}}, which sealed most of the territory, including the coast and the phosphate mines, behind defended lines. The Polisario was left with a thin strip of desert to the east.

By 1991 neither side could win. The UN's [[e:Settlement Plan]] traded a ceasefire for a referendum, and the Security Council created [[p:United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara|MINURSO]] to organise it. The vote foundered on one question: who counts as Sahrawi. Morocco wanted to include people with tribal links who had moved in or lived outside; the Polisario held to the Spanish census of 1974. Each side expected to lose a vote run on the other's list. In 2007 Morocco offered autonomy under its sovereignty instead, and that idea slowly gathered support.

The balance tipped after 2020. A Polisario blockade at Guerguerat brought Moroccan troops into the buffer zone, the Polisario declared the ceasefire dead, and low-level fighting resumed. Weeks later the United States recognised Moroccan sovereignty; Spain, France and Britain later backed the autonomy plan, and in 2025 the Security Council called it the basis for talks. When Russia vetoed a similar US text this October, MINURSO's mandate ran out, and the last neutral witnesses along the berm went home.

timeline.text: Spain claims the coast; the territory later becomes the province of Spanish Sahara.
Sahrawi activists found the [[p:Polisario Front]] to fight Spanish rule.
Morocco's [[e:Green March]] crosses the border; the [[e:Madrid Accords]] hand the territory to Morocco and Mauritania.
The [[e:Western Sahara War]]: Mauritania withdraws in 1979, and Morocco seals most of the territory behind a defended sand wall.
The UN [[e:Settlement Plan]] brings a ceasefire and creates [[p:United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara|MINURSO]]; the referendum stalls over who may vote.
Morocco presents its [[e:Western Sahara autonomy proposal|autonomy plan]] as an alternative to independence.
After a standoff at Guerguerat the Polisario ends the ceasefire ([[e:Western Saharan clashes (2020–present)]]); the US recognises Moroccan sovereignty.
Russia vetoes a US draft backing autonomy, MINURSO's mandate lapses, and the Polisario declares a general mobilisation.

perspectives.view: Morocco sees the Sahara as provinces cut off by colonialism and restored in 1975, pointing to the sultans' historic ties with Saharan tribes. It calls its autonomy plan a generous compromise now backed by major powers, and casts the Polisario as an Algerian-backed proxy.

The Polisario sees Western Sahara as Africa's last unfinished decolonisation: a territory invaded in 1975, whose people were promised a referendum by the UN and denied it. It says autonomy under Morocco cannot replace a free vote that includes independence.

Algeria, which hosts the refugee camps, says it backs self-determination as a matter of principle, not a territorial claim, and rejects being called a party to the conflict, while its rivalry with Morocco shapes the dispute.

keyTerms.meaning: The Hassaniya-speaking people of Western Sahara, now split between the Moroccan-held territory, the Tindouf camps in Algeria and a diaspora.
Morocco's [[p:Moroccan Western Sahara wall|sand wall]], about 2,700 km long, which divides the Moroccan-held west from a Polisario-held strip in the east.
The UN mission created in 1991 to monitor the ceasefire and hold the referendum; its mandate lapsed on 31 October 2026.
Morocco's 2007 offer of self-rule for the territory under Moroccan sovereignty, without an independence option.

items.whyItMatters: For the first time since 1991 no neutral monitor watches the berm, so a single incident, like the disputed drone strike reported near Mijek, could escalate unchecked. The deeper fight over who gets to decide the territory's future is still unresolved, and it is tied up with the Morocco–Algeria rivalry. Watch whether the Security Council returns to the issue, whether Algeria restrains or arms the Polisario, and whether the [[p:African Union]] steps in.

items.title: Why the Crimean Bridge is the war's most symbolic target
items.thread: Russia–Ukraine front line and long-range strikes
items.hook: Russia's huge 20 November air attack on Kyiv's bridges came a day after [[p:Vladimir Putin]] vowed revenge for Ukraine's strikes on the Crimean Bridge. The history of that bridge, from a short-lived wartime crossing to the Kremlin's showpiece, explains why it matters so much more than its traffic.
items.body:
Russia's barrage of 20 November, aimed at bridges over the Dnipro, came after [[p:Vladimir Putin]] vowed revenge for Ukraine's attacks on a bridge of Russia's: the 19-km road and rail link over the Kerch Strait. To see why one structure carries so much weight, start with the water it crosses.

The Kerch Strait, a few kilometres wide, joins the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov and separates Crimea from Russia's Taman peninsula. Rulers have dreamed of bridging it for over a century, but the only fixed crossing before 2018 lasted a few months. German forces began one in 1943 to supply their Kuban bridgehead; after they retreated, the Soviets used the leftover materials to build the [[e:Kerch railway bridge]] {{note: The first train crossed on 3 November 1944; ice floes wrecked its piers in February 1945, and it was dismantled.}}. For the next seven decades, ferries did the job.

In 1954 Moscow moved Crimea from the Russian to the Ukrainian Soviet republic, an administrative change that mattered little until the Soviet Union broke up in 1991. Crimea then belonged to an independent Ukraine, its only land links ran north through the Ukrainian mainland, and the strait became a shared and sometimes quarrelled-over waterway.

That changed in March 2014, when Russia seized and annexed the peninsula in the [[e:Annexation of Crimea by the Russian Federation|annexation of Crimea]], a step most UN members still reject. Crimea was now cut off from Russia by land: Ukraine stopped the canal water and, after activists blew up pylons in 2015, the power. A bridge became the Kremlin's answer and its symbol. [[p:Arkady Rotenberg]] {{note: Childhood judo partner of Vladimir Putin; his Stroygazmontazh firm won the bridge contract in 2015.}} built it for about US$3.7bn, and Putin drove a truck across at the opening of the [[p:Crimean Bridge]] in May 2018; trains followed in December 2019. Within months it showed a military edge too: in the [[e:Kerch Strait incident]] of November 2018, Russia parked a tanker under the span and seized three Ukrainian navy boats.

After the full-scale invasion of 2022, the bridge became a supply line for Russian forces in southern Ukraine, and so a target. On 8 October 2022, the day after Putin's 70th birthday, a truck bomb in the [[e:2022 Crimean Bridge explosion]] dropped part of the roadway. Two days later Russia fired a wave of missiles at Kyiv and Ukraine's power grid, which Putin called retaliation, opening its long [[e:Russian strikes against Ukrainian infrastructure|campaign against Ukraine's energy system]]. Sea drones hit the bridge in the [[e:2023 Crimean Bridge explosion]], killing two civilians, and Ukraine's security service said it set off underwater charges near the piers in June 2025.

Two things blunted the bridge's military value. Russia's capture of the land corridor along the Sea of Azov in 2022 gave Crimea a second road in, and repeated strikes pushed much military cargo onto that route. But the bridge's symbolic weight never faded. That is why the mid-November 2026 strikes, which brought an arch and a stretch of roadway down into the strait, drew a promise of revenge from Putin, and why the answer came as a night of missiles aimed at Kyiv's own bridges, echoing October 2022.

timeline.text: The Soviets open the [[e:Kerch railway bridge]] across the strait; ice destroys it within months, in February 1945.
Crimea is transferred from the Russian to the Ukrainian Soviet republic, and stays with Ukraine at independence in 1991.
Russia annexes Crimea, leaving the peninsula without a land link to Russia.
[[p:Vladimir Putin]] opens the road section of the [[p:Crimean Bridge]]; rail follows in December 2019.
In the [[e:Kerch Strait incident]], Russia blocks the strait under the bridge and seizes three Ukrainian navy boats.
A truck bomb damages the bridge; two days later Russia launches mass missile strikes on Kyiv and the power grid.
Ukrainian sea drones hit the bridge, collapsing a road section and killing two people.
Ukrainian strikes bring down an arch; Russia answers with one of the war's largest air attacks, hitting Kyiv's bridges.

perspectives.view: The bridge reunited Crimea with Russia after what Moscow calls the peninsula's free choice in 2014. Officials describe it as civilian infrastructure and attacks on it as terrorism that justifies retaliation.

Kyiv sees the bridge as an illegal structure built on occupied Ukrainian territory without its consent, and a military supply line for the occupying army. It calls it a legitimate target and its fall a step towards returning Crimea.

Most UN members, through a 2014 General Assembly resolution, regard Crimea as Ukrainian. The EU and US sanctioned the bridge's builders, while debate over whether particular strikes are proportionate continues.

keyTerms.meaning: The narrow channel linking the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, between Crimea and Russia's Taman peninsula. It is the only sea route to Ukraine's Azov ports.
The strip of occupied southern Ukraine along the Sea of Azov that Russia captured in 2022, giving it a road and rail route to Crimea that does not need the bridge.
The construction company of [[p:Arkady Rotenberg]] that built the bridge, later placed under Western sanctions.

items.whyItMatters: Because the bridge is Putin's personal symbol of holding Crimea, strikes on it bring retaliation out of proportion to their military effect, as in October 2022 and again this week. Watch how fast Russia repairs the span, whether it leans more on the Azov land corridor, and whether Moscow keeps targeting Ukraine's own bridges and power plants in answer.

items.title: Why every EU budget ends in a veto fight
items.hook: [[p:António Costa]] has cut the EU's 2028–34 budget plan to win over the frugal states, and [[p:Robert Fico]] says Slovakia won't join a new Ukraine loan that needs all 27. Both moves follow a script written over fifty years of budget fights where every capital holds a veto.
items.body:
Every seven years the EU must agree how much it will spend and on what, and every time the deal comes down to a marathon summit. Next week's meeting on the 2028–34 budget will be no different. The reason is built into the rules: the long-term budget needs the consent of every government, so each one holds a veto, and over five decades members have learned to use it.

The fight began over money flowing back home. In 1970 the Community gave itself "own resources", customs duties, farm levies and later a slice of VAT, so its income no longer depended on yearly handouts from capitals. But most spending went to farm subsidies, and Britain, with a small farm sector and large imports from outside Europe, paid in far more than it received. [[p:Margaret Thatcher]] spent five years demanding her money back until the [[e:UK rebate]] {{note: Agreed at the Fontainebleau European Council in June 1984 and in effect from 1985 until Britain left the EU.}} gave Britain a permanent discount. It set a lasting idea: what a country pays in and gets out can be bargained over.

Endless yearly budget crises led [[p:Jacques Delors]] to a fix. The 1988 Delors package set the first multi-year spending plan, capped spending as a share of national income and doubled regional aid for poorer members. The seven-year cycle and the trade-off at its heart, net payers holding down the total while poorer regions defend cohesion and farm money, grew from there. The [[e:Treaty of Lisbon]] {{note: Signed in Lisbon in December 2007; in force from 1 December 2009.}} wrote the framework into the treaties and kept unanimity.

From then on the vetoes got louder. In 2013 Britain and its allies won the first real-terms cut in a long-term budget. In July 2020, after four days of talks, the Netherlands, Austria, Sweden and Denmark, the so-called frugals, accepted the first large-scale joint borrowing, the [[e:Next Generation EU]] {{note: A €750bn recovery fund agreed by EU leaders in July 2020, financed by borrowing on the markets by the Commission.}} recovery fund, in exchange for bigger rebates of their own. Months later Hungary and Poland held up the whole package over a new link between EU money and the rule of law, until a December compromise.

Ukraine turned the veto into a geopolitical lever. In December 2023 [[p:Viktor Orbán]] blocked €50bn for Kyiv in a budget revision, giving way only in February 2024. In December 2025, when the plan to fund Ukraine from frozen Russian assets stalled, leaders agreed €90bn of joint borrowing for 2026–27 but let Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia stay out of it.

That is the backdrop to this week. [[p:António Costa]] has trimmed the Commission's plan by about 10% to win over the frugals, and a further €45bn for Ukraine in 2027 needs a change to budget rules that every member must accept. [[p:Robert Fico]] calls the link blackmail. The old bargains over national returns now carry the war's cost as well.

timeline.text: The Community gets its own resources (customs duties, farm levies, later a share of VAT) instead of national contributions.
[[p:Margaret Thatcher]] wins the [[e:UK rebate]] at the Fontainebleau summit.
The Delors package creates the first multi-year spending plan and doubles regional aid.
The [[e:Treaty of Lisbon]] makes the [[p:Multiannual Financial Framework]] binding, adopted by unanimity with Parliament's consent.
Leaders agree the first real-terms cut in a long-term budget, for 2014–20.
The frugals accept [[e:Next Generation EU]] joint borrowing for larger rebates; Hungary and Poland hold the package up over rule-of-law conditions.
After the frozen-assets plan stalls, leaders agree €90bn of joint borrowing for Ukraine, with Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia exempted.
Costa tables a 2028–34 budget about 10% below the Commission's plan; Fico rejects a new €45bn Ukraine loan ahead of the 26–27 Nov summit.

perspectives.view: They see themselves as guardians of taxpayers' money: the EU should spend better rather than more, and rebates correct an unfair burden. Joint borrowing in 2020 was a one-off, not a precedent.

perspectives.side: Cohesion countries in the east and south
perspectives.view: For them the budget is the price of the single market, from which richer members profit most. Cutting regional and farm money breaks the bargain that made enlargement and integration work.

perspectives.side: Veto-wielding governments such as Hungary and Slovakia
perspectives.view: They argue unanimity protects national sovereignty and that tying EU money to rule-of-law tests or Ukraine support is political pressure. Critics answer that they use the veto to extract concessions.

keyTerms.meaning: The EU's seven-year spending plan setting ceilings for each area; under the [[e:Treaty of Lisbon]] it needs unanimity in the Council and Parliament's consent.
The EU's revenue streams: customs duties, a share of VAT, contributions based on national income and newer levies such as on unrecycled plastic.
A member that pays more into the EU budget than it receives back in EU spending.
The draft deal the European Council President tables before a budget summit, with figures left for leaders to settle.

items.whyItMatters: Because the budget needs every government's consent, a single capital can hold up both the 2028–34 plan and money for Ukraine. Watch whether leaders strike a deal on 26–27 Nov or push it into 2027, and whether the Ukraine loan again goes ahead with holdouts exempted, a workaround that keeps aid flowing but chips away at the idea of a common budget.

items.title: Why Russia has warships in Libya
items.thread: Russia–Ukraine front line and long-range strikes
items.hook: Ukraine's [[p:Security Service of Ukraine|SBU]] says its sea drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury in Benghazi, far from its home waters in the Black Sea. Russian ships are in eastern Libya because of a relationship with [[p:Khalifa Haftar]] built over a decade of civil war, and made more valuable when Russia's hold on Syria slipped.
items.body:
A Russian warship refuelling in Benghazi is the product of fifteen years of Libyan chaos and one Russian grudge. To see why Moscow's navy is in eastern Libya at all, start with 2011.

That year, as rebels rose against [[p:Muammar Gaddafi]] {{note: An army officer who seized power in a bloodless coup in September 1969 and ruled Libya for 42 years.}}, Russia let the UN Security Council authorise a no-fly zone by abstaining. The [[e:2011 military intervention in Libya]] that followed went far beyond protecting civilians: NATO air power helped topple Gaddafi, who was killed in October. Russian leaders concluded they had been tricked into regime change, and Libya became a standing example in Kremlin speeches of Western overreach. It also cost Russia arms and rail contracts worth billions.

Libya did not settle. In 2014 the country split between rival authorities in Tripoli and the east, and the [[e:Second Libyan Civil War]] began. In the east, [[p:Khalifa Haftar]] {{note: A Gaddafi-era officer who broke with the regime in the 1980s, lived for years in the United States and returned in 2011.}} built the [[p:Libyan National Army]] and courted foreign patrons, among them Egypt, the UAE and, increasingly, Russia. In January 2017 he was received aboard the carrier Admiral Kuznetsov off the Libyan coast, a sign that Moscow saw in him a partner.

The turning point came in 2019. Haftar marched on Tripoli, seat of the UN-recognised [[p:Government of National Accord]], and by autumn fighters of the [[p:Wagner Group]] {{note: A private military company linked to Yevgeny Prigozhin, first seen fighting in eastern Ukraine in 2014.}} were at the front. Turkey answered in early 2020 with drones, advisers and Syrian fighters, and Haftar's siege collapsed. Yet Wagner did not go home. It pulled back to the Jufra air base and the area around Sirte, and in 2020 the US military said Russia had flown in fighter jets. Defeat at Tripoli gave Russia something better than a victory: a lasting presence in the middle of the country.

Two shocks then deepened it. After [[p:Yevgeny Prigozhin]]'s mutiny and death in 2023, the Russian defence ministry took over Wagner's African network, rebranding it the Africa Corps, and Libya became its logistics hub for the Sahel. Then, in December 2024, the [[e:Fall of the Assad regime|fall of the Assad regime]] put Russia's Syrian bases at risk, and equipment began moving to eastern Libya. Analysts now describe Haftar's territory as Russia's most important foothold in the region, with reported work at several air bases and plans for the port of Tobruk.

Ukraine has followed. This year it has struck Russian shipping in the Mediterranean and reportedly operates from western Libya, on the other side of the country's divide. The attack in Benghazi turns Libya's old split between east and west into a front in Europe's war.

timeline.text: Russia abstains on UN Resolution 1973; the [[e:2011 military intervention in Libya]] helps topple [[p:Muammar Gaddafi]], killed in October.
Libya splits between rival authorities in the west and east; [[p:Khalifa Haftar]] launches his campaign in the east.
Haftar is received aboard the Russian carrier Admiral Kuznetsov off Libya.
Haftar's offensive on Tripoli draws in the [[p:Wagner Group]]; Turkish support for the government breaks the siege, and Wagner withdraws to Jufra and Sirte.
After [[p:Yevgeny Prigozhin]]'s mutiny and death, the Russian defence ministry absorbs Wagner's Libyan operations into its Africa Corps.
The [[e:Fall of the Assad regime|fall of the Assad regime]] threatens Russia's Syrian bases; equipment begins moving to eastern Libya.
Ukraine strikes Russian shipping in the Mediterranean and is reported to operate from western Libya.
A blast destroys a Russian warship at Benghazi; Ukraine claims sea drones sank the corvette Merkury.

perspectives.view: Moscow tells this story as one of Western recklessness: NATO's 2011 campaign destroyed the Libyan state, and Russia now works with Libyan authorities to restore stability. It long denied any state role for Wagner and calls its current ties ordinary military cooperation.

The [[p:Libyan National Army]] presents itself as the force that defeated terrorists and militias, and its foreign partnerships as a sovereign choice. It condemned the Benghazi strike as a violation of Libyan sovereignty.

They see a foothold Russia gained through mercenaries and a divided country, now used to supply its operations in Africa and move sanctioned cargo. Kyiv says Russian military assets are legitimate targets wherever they are.

keyTerms.meaning: The March 2011 UN Security Council resolution authorising a no-fly zone and 'all necessary measures' to protect Libyan civilians; Russia and China abstained.
The armed coalition led by [[p:Khalifa Haftar]] that controls most of eastern and southern Libya.
The Russian defence ministry structure that took over most of Wagner's operations in Africa after 2023.
An air base in central Libya that became the main hub for Russian forces after the 2020 retreat from Tripoli.

items.whyItMatters: Russia's position in eastern Libya gives it a Mediterranean foothold on NATO's southern flank and a supply route to the Sahel, which matters more now that its Syrian bases are uncertain. A Ukrainian strike there exposes those ships and tests [[p:Khalifa Haftar]]'s balancing between Moscow and the West. Watch whether Russia reinforces air defences in Libya, how Tripoli responds to reports of Ukrainians on its side, and whether the strike affects US-led peace talks.

items.title: Why Iran ties Hormuz to sanctions: 75 years of economic war over Iranian oil
items.hook: Tehran says Hormuz reopens only if the US lifts both the [[e:2026 United States naval blockade of Iran|naval blockade]] and its sanctions, while [[p:Donald Trump]] threatens to sink any ship that runs the blockade. Behind that demand lies a long history in which Western pressure on Iran has been, above all, pressure on its oil.
items.body:
Iran's spokesman says the Strait of Hormuz reopens only when the blockade and the sanctions end. To see why Tehran ties the two together, go back 75 years: for most of that time the fight between Iran and the West has been a fight over who gets to sell Iran's oil.

It began with the [[e:Abadan Crisis]]. {{note: Began in 1951 when Iran's parliament nationalised the British-owned Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, whose refinery at Abadan was then among the world's largest.}} Prime Minister [[p:Mohammad Mosaddegh]] took over the oil industry, and Britain answered with a worldwide boycott of Iranian oil, backed by its navy in the Gulf. Iran's exports collapsed. The standoff ended not in a deal but in the [[e:1953 Iranian coup d'état]], organised by the CIA and Britain's MI6. Many Iranians still read every later embargo through that memory: economic pressure first, regime change after.

The modern sanctions era opened with the [[e:Iran hostage crisis]]. {{note: Began on 4 November 1979, when student followers of Ayatollah Khomeini seized the US embassy in Tehran and held 52 Americans for 444 days.}} Jimmy Carter froze Iranian assets in the United States, and the [[e:Algiers Accords]] that freed the hostages in January 1981 unwound only part of that. Through the 1980s Washington banned imports of Iranian goods, while the Tanker War, the subject of an earlier lesson, showed that Iran's oil could also be fought over at sea.

The turning point was the move from American to global pressure. In 1995 Bill Clinton banned almost all US trade with Iran, and the next year Congress passed the [[e:Iran and Libya Sanctions Act]], which threatened foreign companies that invested in Iran's energy sector. That reach beyond US borders, now called secondary sanctions, became Washington's main weapon. As fears about Iran's nuclear programme grew, the UN joined in, most heavily with [[e:United Nations Security Council Resolution 1929|Resolution 1929]] in 2010. In 2012 the EU stopped buying Iranian oil and Iranian banks were cut off from the SWIFT payments network. Iran's oil exports fell by roughly half.

That pain brought Tehran to the [[e:Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action]] in 2015, which traded limits on its nuclear work for sanctions relief. The relief proved short-lived. In May 2018 Donald Trump withdrew and launched a "maximum pressure" campaign aimed at driving Iran's oil sales towards zero, and in September 2025 Britain, France and Germany triggered the return of UN sanctions. {{note: The 'snapback' mechanism was written into the 2015 deal and endorsed by UN Security Council Resolution 2231.}}

The 2026 war turned economic pressure into force. After Iran closed Hormuz, the US imposed the [[e:2026 United States naval blockade of Iran|naval blockade]] in April: a blockade does at sea what sanctions had tried to do through banks. The June memorandum from the [[e:Islamabad Talks]] lifted it, but Washington reimposed the blockade in July and now rejects the memorandum. Seen from Tehran, reopening the strait without sanctions relief would mean giving up its one counterweight to seventy years of being squeezed.

timeline.text: Iran nationalises its oil industry; Britain answers with a worldwide boycott in the [[e:Abadan Crisis]].
A CIA- and MI6-backed coup topples [[p:Mohammad Mosaddegh]].
After the US embassy is seized, Washington freezes Iranian assets; the [[e:Algiers Accords]] partly unwind the freeze in 1981.
A US trade embargo, then the [[e:Iran and Libya Sanctions Act]], begin the era of secondary sanctions on foreign firms.
UN [[e:United Nations Security Council Resolution 1929|Resolution 1929]], an EU oil embargo and a SWIFT cut-off roughly halve Iran's oil exports.
The [[e:Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action]] brings sanctions relief; the US withdraws in May 2018 and launches 'maximum pressure'.
The US blockades Iran in April, lifts it under the June Islamabad memorandum, and reimposes it in July.
Trump threatens to sink blockade runners; Iran demands an end to sanctions and the blockade before Hormuz reopens.

perspectives.view: Tehran tells this as one continuous story, from the 1951 boycott and the 1953 coup to 'maximum pressure' and the blockade: outside powers using its oil to punish or overthrow it. It argues that sanctions are economic warfare, so lifting them is a fair condition for reopening the strait.

Washington says sanctions answered Iranian actions, from hostage-taking to support for armed groups and a nuclear programme it believes aimed at a bomb. It sees the blockade as a response to Iran closing an international waterway, and refuses to pay for reopening it with sanctions relief.

Britain, France and Germany long defended the 2015 deal and tried to keep trade with Iran after the US left it. They triggered UN snapback in 2025 over Iran's nuclear steps, but back the Islamabad memorandum and free passage through Hormuz.

keyTerms.meaning: Penalties on companies and banks from other countries that do business with a sanctioned state, used by the US against Iran since the [[e:Iran and Libya Sanctions Act]] of 1996.
A clause of the 2015 nuclear deal letting any party restore the old UN sanctions; Britain, France and Germany used it, and the sanctions returned in September 2025.
Using warships to stop shipping to or from an enemy's ports. Under the laws of war it is an act of war, which is why Iran calls the US blockade military aggression.
The 14-point US–Iran memorandum of June 2026, brokered by Pakistan and Qatar after the [[e:Islamabad Talks]], which ended the blockade and reopened Hormuz for a time.

items.whyItMatters: Because both sides read today's standoff through decades of sanctions, neither sees the strait as a separate issue: Washington will not trade sanctions relief for reopening it, and Tehran will not reopen it without relief. Watch whether the convoy of tankers off Kharg Island tries to run the blockade, and whether Qatar's mediation can revive the Islamabad memorandum before a clash at sea forces the question.

items.title: How the Rohingya were written out of Myanmar, and how a small African state took the case to The Hague
items.hook: The [[p:International Court of Justice]] has found Myanmar responsible for the [[e:Rohingya genocide]], the first time it has ruled that a state committed genocide. The violence it judged, in 2017, was the end point of decades in which Myanmar's rulers stripped the Rohingya of citizenship and called them foreigners.
items.body:
When the [[p:International Court of Justice]] ruled on 19 November that Myanmar was responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, it closed a case that took seven years. The roots of what it judged go back much further: to a long argument over whether the Rohingya belong in Myanmar at all.

The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim people of northern Rakhine, the coastal region once ruled by the kingdom of Arakan. Muslims lived there for centuries, but under British rule, after the [[e:First Anglo-Burmese War]] gave Britain the region in 1826, many more arrived from neighbouring Bengal. That mixed history is the core of the dispute. Rohingya see themselves as natives of Arakan; Myanmar's nationalists, and successive governments, call them "Bengalis" who came with the colonisers. Violence between Rakhine Buddhists and Muslims during the Second World War hardened the divide.

The turning point came after [[p:Ne Win]] seized power in 1962 and built a state around Burman Buddhist identity. In 1978 [[e:Operation Dragon King]] {{note: An army-run census and immigration drive launched in Rakhine in February 1978 to register citizens and screen out "foreigners".}} sent some 200,000 Rohingya fleeing to Bangladesh; most were later sent back. Then came the decisive blow: the 1982 citizenship law listed the "national races" entitled to full citizenship, and the Rohingya were not among them. Most became stateless in the only country they knew, needing permission to travel, marry or study. Another 250,000 fled in 1991–92.

Myanmar's partial opening after 2011 made things worse, not better. Freer speech let anti-Muslim nationalism spread, and the [[e:2012 Rakhine State riots]] drove around 140,000 people, most of them Rohingya, into closed camps. A small armed group, the [[p:Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army]], {{note: Emerged in 2016 under Ata Ullah, a Rohingya born in Pakistan and raised in Saudi Arabia; it first attacked border posts in October 2016.}} attacked police posts in October 2016 and again on 25 August 2017. The army's answer, which it called "clearance operations", burned hundreds of villages and killed thousands. More than 700,000 Rohingya escaped to Bangladesh within months, where nearly a million now live in camps around Cox's Bazar.

Myanmar was then led by a civilian government under [[p:Aung San Suu Kyi]], but the army under [[p:Min Aung Hlaing]] ran the operations. In 2018 UN investigators said the generals should be investigated for genocide. In November 2019 The Gambia, a small West African state backed by the [[p:Organisation of Islamic Cooperation]], sued Myanmar under the [[e:Genocide Convention]], {{note: Adopted by the UN General Assembly in December 1948, after the Holocaust; it lets any party take another to the ICJ over disputes about genocide.}} arguing that every party has an interest in preventing genocide. Suu Kyi went to The Hague herself to defend her country. In January 2020 the court ordered Myanmar to protect the Rohingya; a year later Min Aung Hlaing ousted her in the [[e:2021 Myanmar coup d'état]].

The ruling matters because the court has been very reluctant to find states guilty. In 2007 it held Serbia responsible only for failing to prevent the [[e:Srebrenica massacre]], not for committing genocide. The [[e:Rohingya genocide case]] is the first time it has found a state itself responsible, and the first time a country with no direct stake brought such a case and won.

timeline.text: Britain takes Arakan after the [[e:First Anglo-Burmese War]]; migration from Bengal grows under colonial rule.
[[e:Operation Dragon King]] drives about 200,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh.
A new citizenship law leaves the Rohingya off the list of national races, making most of them stateless.
The [[e:2012 Rakhine State riots]] push about 140,000 people, mostly Rohingya, into camps.
After [[p:Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army|ARSA]] attacks, army "clearance operations" drive more than 700,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh.
The Gambia sues Myanmar at the ICJ under the [[e:Genocide Convention]]; provisional measures follow in January 2020.
[[p:Min Aung Hlaing]] seizes power in the [[e:2021 Myanmar coup d'état]]; the junta keeps defending the case.
The ICJ finds Myanmar responsible for genocide and orders prosecutions, guarantees of non-repetition and safe return.

perspectives.view: The Rohingya are an indigenous people of Arakan with centuries of history there. Decades of denied citizenship, restrictions and periodic expulsions culminated in 2017 in killings carried out with intent to destroy the group, which is genocide.

The people it calls Bengalis are largely migrants from the colonial era and after, not one of the national races. The 2017 operations were counter-terrorism against [[p:Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army|ARSA]]; abuses, where they happened, are for national courts, and genocidal intent was never shown.

Rakhine Buddhists see themselves as a threatened minority in their own homeland, squeezed between Burman rule and a growing Muslim population next to Bangladesh, and point to wartime and later violence against their own community.

keyTerms.meaning: Myanmar's nationality law that grants full citizenship to listed "national races" and those who can prove ancestry before 1823; the Rohingya were left off the list.
The 1948 treaty defining genocide as acts committed with intent to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group, in whole or in part.
Duties owed to all parties of a treaty, which is why The Gambia, without being directly harmed, could bring the case.
The Myanmar army's term for its 2016–17 campaigns in northern Rakhine.
The Bangladeshi district where nearly a million Rohingya refugees live in camps, including Kutupalong, among the world's largest.

items.whyItMatters: The ruling binds Myanmar but the court cannot enforce it; that falls to the UN Security Council, where China and Russia have shielded the junta. Watch whether [[p:Min Aung Hlaing]]'s government answers by pulling away from [[p:ASEAN]], how the ICC's separate case against him moves, and whether the judgment changes anything for the Rohingya in Bangladesh's camps, who still cannot go home safely.

items.title: Section 301: the 1974 trade law Washington uses as a crowbar
items.hook: The new 15–35% tariffs proposed on 14 economies rest on [[e:Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974|Section 301]], a law Washington used to pry open Japan's markets in the 1980s and to start its trade war with China in 2018. After the Supreme Court took away the emergency route to tariffs in February, it has become the administration's main weapon.
items.body:
On 25 November the [[p:Office of the United States Trade Representative|US trade representative's office]] proposed tariffs of 15 to 35 percent on 14 economies, among them America's closest allies. The legal tool it reached for is half a century old, and its history explains both why Washington chose it and why trading partners distrust it.

Section 301 was written into the [[e:Trade Act of 1974]] {{note: Signed by President Gerald Ford in January 1975, the act also created fast-track trade negotiating authority.}} at a time when Congress felt the postwar trading rules, the [[p:General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade]], were too slow to stop foreign practices hurting American exporters. It lets the president's trade office investigate any foreign policy it judges unreasonable, unjustifiable or discriminatory, and then retaliate with tariffs or other limits. Crucially, Washington itself is investigator, judge and enforcer.

The law came into its own in the 1980s, when Japan's rise and a soaring trade deficit alarmed Congress. A Section 301 case over Japanese chips led to a 1986 semiconductor agreement, and when Washington decided Tokyo was not honouring it, [[p:Ronald Reagan]] imposed 100 percent tariffs in 1987 on about $300 million of Japanese electronics. In 1988 Congress went further with **Super 301**, which obliged the trade office to name priority countries for action; Japan, Brazil and India were named in 1989. To admirers this was a crowbar that opened closed markets. To its targets it was bullying.

The creation of the [[p:World Trade Organization]] in 1995 seemed to retire the crowbar. The new body had binding dispute settlement, and the United States promised to take its complaints there instead. When the EU challenged Section 301, a WTO panel in 2000 let it stand mainly because Washington had pledged to use it within WTO rules. For two decades it was rarely used to raise tariffs.

That changed in 2017, when [[p:Donald Trump]] ordered a Section 301 probe into China's treatment of American technology and intellectual property. Tariffs followed from July 2018 and, through rounds of retaliation, the [[e:China–United States trade war]] came to cover roughly $370 billion of Chinese goods. A WTO panel ruled against the tariffs in 2020, but the US appealed to an appeals body that no longer had enough judges to sit, so the ruling never took effect. The Biden administration kept the tariffs and raised some, notably on Chinese electric vehicles in 2024.

This year the law moved to centre stage again. On 20 February the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that the emergency-powers law behind most of Trump's 2025 tariffs did not authorise tariffs at all. The administration bridged the gap with a temporary tariff that the law caps at 150 days, and on 11 March opened Section 301 investigations into "structural excess capacity" in 16 economies. Because Section 301 tariffs have survived court challenges and depend on no emergency, they are the sturdiest tool left. This week's proposals, and a separate one on Brazilian aircraft from an earlier Brazil case, are the result.

timeline.text: Congress passes the [[e:Trade Act of 1974]], whose Section 301 lets the president retaliate against unfair foreign trade practices.
[[p:Ronald Reagan]] imposes 100% tariffs on about $300m of Japanese electronics in a semiconductor dispute.
"Super 301" forces the trade office to name priority countries; Japan, Brazil and India are listed.
The [[p:World Trade Organization]] opens; the US promises to bring disputes there, and Section 301 goes largely quiet.
Section 301 tariffs on Chinese goods launch the [[e:China–United States trade war]].
The Supreme Court rules 6–3 that the emergency-powers law does not authorise tariffs.
USTR opens Section 301 probes into excess manufacturing capacity in 16 economies.
USTR proposes 15–35% tariffs on 14 economies and a 10% tariff on Brazilian aircraft; hearings start 25 January.

perspectives.view: Section 301 is the tool Congress gave the president to answer foreign subsidies and overcapacity that WTO rules have failed to restrain. Its record with Japan and China shows that only the threat of tariffs brings partners to the table.

perspectives.side: Targeted trading partners (EU, China, Brazil and others)
perspectives.view: It lets one country act as accuser, judge and enforcer, bypassing the WTO system the US helped build. Brasília calls the aircraft tariff illegal, and several partners have threatened to retaliate.
Section 301 tariffs are paid mostly by American firms and consumers, and decades of use have not closed trade deficits. Congress, they argue, has handed too much tariff power to the executive.

keyTerms.meaning: Part of the [[e:Trade Act of 1974]] that lets the US trade representative investigate foreign practices and impose tariffs or other retaliation.
A 1988 add-on that required the trade office to name priority countries and practices each year for possible action; it has lapsed and been revived several times.
The administration's term for state-driven production beyond what home markets can absorb, which then floods export markets; the basis of the 2026 investigations.
A provision of the same 1974 act allowing a temporary tariff of up to 15% for at most 150 days to deal with balance-of-payments problems; used as a bridge after the February ruling.

items.whyItMatters: Section 301 gives Washington tariffs that courts have upheld and that need no emergency, so it is likely to carry US trade policy for years. Watch the hearings from 25 January, whether the EU, Japan or Brazil retaliate or strike deals first, and whether Canada and Mexico, spared for now, end up in a later round.

items.title: Why Uganda keeps sending its army into Congo
items.hook: Uganda's army chief [[p:Muhoozi Kainerugaba]] says he ordered troops into eastern Congo and backs the FRN rebels. Uganda has been in Congo before: as an invader in 1998, as an occupier condemned by the world court, and since 2021 as Kinshasa's invited partner.
items.body:
When Uganda's army chief says he has ordered troops into eastern Congo, he is describing something Uganda has done, in one form or another, for most of the past thirty years. The story starts in 1996. After the Rwandan genocide, the génocidaires had regrouped in camps in Zaire, and Rwanda and Uganda backed a rebel coalition that marched across the country in the [[e:First Congo War]] and drove out [[p:Mobutu Sese Seko]] in May 1997. They installed [[p:Laurent-Désiré Kabila]]; his son Joseph fought in that campaign.

The alliance soured within a year. In August 1998 Kabila told his Rwandan backers to leave, and Rwanda and Uganda invaded again, starting the [[e:Second Congo War]], which drew in armies from at least six countries. Uganda sponsored its own rebels, chiefly [[p:Movement for the Liberation of the Congo|Jean-Pierre Bemba's MLC]] {{note: Founded in 1998 in northern Congo by businessman Jean-Pierre Bemba, with Ugandan support.}}, and occupied much of the north-east. The two patrons soon fell out over territory and minerals: their armies fought each other in Kisangani three times, most destructively in the [[e:Six-Day War (2000)|Six-Day War]] of June 2000.

Occupation left deep marks in Ituri, a gold-rich province where Ugandan officers backed and armed rival Hema and Lendu factions. A 2001 UN expert panel accused senior Ugandan officers of plundering gold, timber and coffee. The [[e:Ituri conflict]] killed tens of thousands; when Uganda withdrew in May 2003, a French-led EU force, [[e:Operation Artemis]], had to be flown into Bunia to stop massacres.

Kinshasa took Uganda to the International Court of Justice. In December 2005 the court found that Uganda had violated Congo's sovereignty, occupied Ituri and was responsible for abuses and looting. Agreeing on damages took until February 2022, when the court ordered Uganda to pay $325 million in five yearly instalments, far below Congo's claim.

By then Ugandan soldiers were back, this time invited. The [[p:Allied Democratic Forces]] {{note: Ugandan rebel group formed in the mid-1990s; it moved into Congo's Rwenzori borderlands and later pledged loyalty to Islamic State.}} were blamed for suicide bombings in Kampala in November 2021, and on 30 November Uganda and Congo launched [[e:Operation Shujaa]], a joint campaign that put Ugandan troops in North Kivu and Ituri. Researchers noted that the deployment also guarded roads and trade routes useful to Ugandan business.

That dual record explains Kinshasa's alarm now. [[p:Muhoozi Kainerugaba]] {{note: Son of President Yoweri Museveni; made Uganda's Chief of Defence Forces in March 2024.}} has long used social media to make statements his government later softens. But his public support for the [[p:Joseph Kabila]]-led FRN, and his description of Rwanda and Uganda as twin countries, echo 1998, when the two neighbours backed rebels against a Kinshasa government they had once supported. Congo has to decide whether Uganda is a partner against the ADF or a patron of its enemies, and history suggests it can be both.

timeline.text: Rwanda and Uganda back the rebellion that topples Mobutu in the [[e:First Congo War]].
After Laurent Kabila expels his Rwandan allies, Rwanda and Uganda invade again, starting the [[e:Second Congo War]].
Ugandan and Rwandan armies fight each other in Kisangani in the [[e:Six-Day War (2000)|Six-Day War]].
Uganda withdraws from Ituri; the EU's [[e:Operation Artemis]] deploys to Bunia to halt massacres.
The International Court of Justice rules that Uganda violated Congo's sovereignty and looted its resources.
After bombings in Kampala, Uganda and Congo launch the joint [[e:Operation Shujaa]] against the [[p:Allied Democratic Forces]].
The world court sets Uganda's reparations at $325 million, payable over five years.
[[p:Muhoozi Kainerugaba]] publicly backs the FRN rebels and says he ordered troops into Congo; Kinshasa summons Uganda's envoy.

perspectives.view: Uganda says it went into Congo to deal with rebels who used a lawless border to attack it, from the 1990s to the [[p:Allied Democratic Forces]] today. It points out that Operation Shujaa was agreed with Kinshasa and has weakened a group linked to Islamic State.

Kinshasa sees a neighbour that invaded, sponsored rebels and looted its resources, which the world court confirmed in 2005. It treats Ugandan backing for armed groups as a repeat of 1998 and wants Kampala to state its official position.

Many analysts say security and economic interests have always been mixed: Ugandan deployments protected trade routes, gold flows and infrastructure as well as fighting rebels. They disagree on how far Kampala's leaders directed these interests and how far individual officers pursued them.

keyTerms.meaning: Gold-rich province in north-eastern Congo bordering Uganda, occupied by Ugandan forces from 1998 to 2003 and scene of the [[e:Ituri conflict]].
Uganda People's Defence Force, Uganda's army, commanded since 2024 by [[p:Muhoozi Kainerugaba]].
Congo's case against Uganda at the International Court of Justice, decided in 2005, with reparations set in 2022.

items.whyItMatters: Kinshasa already faces Rwanda-linked rebels in the Kivus. If Uganda moves from fighting the ADF alongside Congo to backing the FRN, Congo could again face both neighbours, as it did in 1998. Watch whether Kampala's government distances itself from Muhoozi's posts, whether Ugandan troops move beyond Operation Shujaa's zones, and whether Congo questions Uganda's role in that operation.

items.title: Why a line in Armenia's constitution stands between it and peace with Azerbaijan
items.hook: [[p:Nikol Pashinyan]]'s draft constitution drops its reference to Armenia's 1990 Declaration of Independence, the condition Azerbaijan set for signing their peace treaty. That reference carries a 1989 vote to unite Nagorno-Karabakh with Armenia, which is why Baku treats it as a territorial claim.
items.body:
Armenia's constitution says little about Nagorno-Karabakh directly. The dispute sits in one line of its preamble, which grounds the state in "the fundamental principles of Armenian statehood" set out in the 1990 Declaration of Independence. To see why Baku cares about that line, you have to go back to the last years of the Soviet Union.

In 1923 the Bolsheviks drew Nagorno-Karabakh, a mountain district with an Armenian majority, as an autonomous region inside Soviet Azerbaijan. Armenians resented the arrangement for decades, but under Moscow's rule it stayed frozen. Gorbachev's reforms thawed it. In February 1988 the regional council voted to ask for transfer to Soviet Armenia, and mass rallies in Yerevan became the [[p:Karabakh movement]] {{note: A mass movement launched in Yerevan in February 1988; its leaders' committee later formed the Pan-Armenian National Movement under Levon Ter-Petrosyan.}}. Days later came the [[e:Sumgait pogrom]] against Armenians in an Azerbaijani industrial town, and the conflict turned violent on both sides, with expulsions of Armenians from Azerbaijan and Azerbaijanis from Armenia.

On **1 December 1989** the parliament of Soviet Armenia and Karabakh's Armenian council passed a joint resolution proclaiming the region's "reunification" with Armenia. Moscow annulled it, but it became a founding text. When Armenia's new parliament, led by [[p:Levon Ter-Petrosyan]], adopted its [[e:Declaration of Independence|Declaration of State Sovereignty of Armenia]] on 23 August 1990, the preamble cited that joint decision. The declaration also called for international recognition of the 1915 genocide and referred to Western Armenia, the eastern Anatolian lands now in Turkey.

The [[e:First Nagorno-Karabakh War]] followed independence. By the May 1994 ceasefire, Armenian forces held Karabakh and seven surrounding Azerbaijani districts, and hundreds of thousands of Azerbaijanis had been displaced. Armenia's 1995 constitution tied itself to the 1990 declaration in its preamble, and the 2005 and 2015 revisions kept that wording. For Armenians it was a statement of national origins; for Azerbaijan it was a standing territorial claim written into the supreme law.

The balance of power then reversed. Azerbaijan retook most of the territory in the [[e:Second Nagorno-Karabakh War]] of 2020, and in September 2023 a one-day [[e:2023 Azerbaijani offensive in Nagorno-Karabakh|offensive]] ended the breakaway [[p:Republic of Artsakh]]; almost the entire Armenian population, more than 100,000 people, fled to Armenia. [[p:Nikol Pashinyan]] has since recognised Karabakh as part of Azerbaijan and argues Armenia needs a new constitution without the old preamble.

Baku has kept the preamble on its list of conditions. In 2024 Armenia's Constitutional Court cleared the rules for border demarcation and played down the preamble's legal force, but Azerbaijan said only a new text would do. The two sides finished negotiating a peace treaty in March 2025 and initialled it at the White House in August, but [[p:Ilham Aliyev]] says he will not sign until the constitution changes. Pashinyan's draft is meant to meet that demand; whether he can get it to a referendum is a separate fight.

timeline.text: Soviet authorities create the Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Oblast, an Armenian-majority region inside Soviet Azerbaijan.
Karabakh's regional council asks to join Soviet Armenia; the [[p:Karabakh movement]] fills Yerevan's squares and violence follows.
Soviet Armenia's parliament and Karabakh's Armenian council jointly proclaim the region's "reunification" with Armenia.
Armenia's [[e:Declaration of State Sovereignty of Armenia|Declaration of Independence]] cites the 1989 joint decision in its preamble.
Armenia's first post-Soviet constitution grounds itself in the 1990 declaration; later revisions keep the reference.
An Azerbaijani [[e:2023 Azerbaijani offensive in Nagorno-Karabakh|offensive]] ends the breakaway republic; more than 100,000 Armenians flee.
Pashinyan and [[p:Ilham Aliyev]] initial the agreed peace treaty at the White House; Baku makes signing conditional on a new Armenian constitution.
Pashinyan publishes a draft constitution without the preamble reference, but lacks the 70 votes needed to call a referendum.

perspectives.view: Baku sees the preamble as a legal claim to its territory that a future Armenian government could revive. It argues that a treaty signed while the claim stays in the constitution would mean nothing, so the text must go first.

Pashinyan's government says Armenia has no territorial claims and has recognised Azerbaijan's borders, but accepts that a new constitution fit for an independent, peaceful state should not lean on Soviet-era documents.

Opposition parties see the 1990 declaration as the founding act of the Armenian state and of the Karabakh cause. They call dropping it a humiliating concession made under pressure, with no guarantee Baku will not ask for more.

keyTerms.meaning: Adopted on 23 August 1990, it began Armenia's break from the USSR. Its preamble cites the 1989 Karabakh reunification decision; independence itself followed a referendum in September 1991.
The opening statement of a constitution. Armenia's grounds the state in the principles of the 1990 declaration, which is how the Karabakh reference reaches the constitution.
The Armenian name for Nagorno-Karabakh, and the name of the unrecognised [[p:Republic of Artsakh]] that existed from 1991 until it dissolved after the 2023 offensive.
In Armenia a new constitution must be approved by voters, and putting it to a vote needs 70 of the 105 MPs.

items.whyItMatters: The treaty text is agreed, so the constitution is now the main legal obstacle to a signed peace. Pashinyan's [[p:Civil Contract (Armenia)|Civil Contract]] has 64 seats and needs six more to call the referendum. Watch whether any opposition MPs cross over, whether Baku adds new conditions, and whether voters, many of them displaced from Karabakh, would approve the change.
